introduction.p: The exponential model P\prime=rP, with r>0, allows a positive population to grow without bound. To model limited resources, the logistic equation reduces the per-capita growth rate as the population approaches a carrying capacity.

subsection.p: The carrying capacity is the level the environment can support in the model.
The first factor says that more individuals create more possible growth. The second factor says that limited resources reduce growth as P approaches K.

exercise.title: Why does the factor 1-P/K slow growth near the carrying capacity?

subsection.title: Population and spread models
subsection.p: The logistic equation appears whenever two ideas are both reasonable:
For populations, the current amount is the population P, and the limiting factor is the carrying capacity K.
For a rumor, the current amount may be the number of people who have heard it. The limiting factor is the number of people who have not yet heard it.

The rumor spreads slowly at first because few people know it. It then spreads quickly when many people know it and many people remain to hear it. Finally it slows again because most people have already heard it.
This slow--fast--slow shape is the signature of a logistic curve.

subsection.title: What logistic models assume
subsection.p: The logistic model is more realistic than pure exponential growth, but it is still a model.
Those assumptions may be useful, but they are not automatic.

paragraphs.title: Warning example: early data can be misleading
paragraphs.p: So early logistic growth and exponential growth can look almost the same.
That means early data may reveal r, but it may not reveal K. To estimate the carrying capacity, we need data from the stage where growth begins to slow.

note.title: Check the model’s assumptions
note.p: Exponential growth assumes a constant relative growth rate.
Logistic growth assumes a fixed carrying capacity and a relative growth rate r(1-P/K), approximately r when P\ll K.
Check whether these assumptions describe the situation before using the model to predict its behavior.

paragraphs.p: This chapter used derivatives to answer practical questions: rates related to rates, best choices, local approximations, root finding, and models whose laws are written as differential equations.

But we have postponed the other half of calculus. If a derivative tells how fast something changes, how do we recover the total change? If velocity is known at every instant, how do we rebuild distance?
That question leads back to the first chapter, where area under a velocity graph was waiting for us. The next chapter begins the integral.

exercise.title: Why can early data hide the carrying capacity?

statement.p: When P\ll K, the logistic model closely approximates exponential growth. Explain why early data may estimate r while providing little information about K.

hint.p: To estimate the ceiling, we need data from the stage where growth begins to slow. Before that, the slowing factor is nearly invisible.
